proxy_language: Hittite (Nesite), with Luwian and Hattic substrate vocabulary for divine and cultic terms
proxy_rationale: The 'Thousand Gods of Hatti' is the standard Hittite self-description of its pantheon, invoked in treaties and state rituals, so cuneiform Hittite (Old, Middle and Neo-Hittite, c. 1650-1180 BCE) is the directly attested language. Divine names and cult terms often come from Hattic (e.g. Wurunsemu, Taru, Kasku) and Luwian (Tarhunna, Kamrusepa, Santa), which a specialist would mix in; Hurrian (Teshub, Hebat, Kumarbi) is also common in the Empire-period court.
phonology: Consonants: stops p, t, k (written single vs double, i.e. voiceless vs voiced-ish lenis/fortis contrast: -p- vs -pp-, -t- vs -tt-, -k- vs -kk-), fricatives s, h (velar/uvular, written h and hh), z (/ts/), affricate z, sonorants m, n, l, r, glides w, y. Vowels a, e, i, u (with long vowels sometimes marked by plene spelling: a-a, e-e etc.). No b, d, g in native words as phonemes (cuneiform signs BA/DA/GA are used for p/t/k; foreign names may show d, b, g). Laryngeal h (from PIE *h2, *h3) is retained as hh. Typical Anatolian features: no feminine gender, only animate/inanimate.
phonotactics: Syllable shapes in cuneiform: V, CV, VC, CVC. Initial consonant clusters are rare in native words but occur (e.g. sp-, st-, tr- spelled with epenthetic vowels). Medial clusters common (-nt-, -rk-, -sk-, -tt-, -hh-, -ks-, -nk-). Word-final consonants are restricted mostly to -s, -n, -r, -z, -t, -k, -l, -m (nominative -s, accusative -n, ablative -az, ergative -anza). Native words do not begin with r, and rarely with l. Geminates are common between vowels.
orthography: Standard Hittitological transliteration: Hittite words in lowercase italic with hyphens between syllabic signs (e.g. a-pa-a-as), with 's' for both s and sh, 'sz' avoided; use ś/š only in Akkadographic or Hurrian contexts. Plene vowels often reduced to simple vowels for game use. Sumerograms in capitals (DINGIR 'god', LUGAL 'king', E 'house') and Akkadograms are not to be used in names. For a Latin-script game: h and hh for the laryngeal, z for /ts/, s for /s/ (not sh), double consonants for geminates, w and y as glides, no k/g/p/b contrast except as in the roots below.
morphology: Indo-European, suffixing. Two genders (animate, inanimate), singular/plural, eight cases (nominative -s/-as, accusative -n/-an, genitive -as/-an, dative-locative -i/-a, allative -a, ablative -az/-az, instrumental -it, ergative -anza). Verbs: present/preterite, imperative, medio-passive; conjugations in -mi and -hi. Derivational suffixes: -ant- (possessor, e.g. watar > wataranta 'watery'), -ahh- (factitive 'to make'), -ess- (inchoative), -ala/-alla (agent/relational), -atar/-ar (abstract/verbal noun), -i-/-ia- (adjectival), -ili (adverbial 'in the manner of', as in nesili 'in Nesite'). Hatti-origin and Luwian words keep their own endings (Luwian nom. -s, plural -nzi; Hattic prefix/suffix system with prefix wa-, le-, ta-, fa-, suffix -ah, -ur).
compounding: True compounds are rare in Hittite; relations are expressed by juxtaposition, genitive constructions, or adjectival derivation. 'X of Y' = Y in genitive before head noun X (e.g. dankuiyas tekan 'of dark earth' = 'dark earth' as genitive; DINGIR-LIM-as ... 'of the god'). Possessor adjective in -ant- before the noun. Agent nouns in -ala- or from verbs with -ant-. Place names built with genitive or the Luwian/Hattic type '[deity name]-ssa' (-ssa- Luwian adjective suffix, '-ssa/-ssi' 'of X'). Divine names are often single-word compounds or epithets: Tarhunna 'Storm', Tarhunna-ssa, UTU-s 'Sun-god'.
noun_phrase_order: Adjective + noun, genitive + head noun (Genitive-Noun), demonstrative + noun, numeral + noun. Genitive and adjective agree in case/number/gender with head where inflected. Postpositions: -sa(n) 'upon', -kan, -an 'on' (clause-initial particles), -za reflexive. In a simplified name builder, use bare stems with appropriate nominative -s or -as, or stem + -ant- for adjectives.

notes: No word may be identical to a Modern Irish, Scottish Gaelic or Manx word (this culture is not Goidelic). The current game names look pseudo-Hurrian/Turkic (sh, -yi, -ulun) and should be replaced; avoid sh, b, d, g, f, o in native-style Hittite words (o does not occur in cuneiform Hittite). For divine names borrow attested forms (Tarhunna, Kamrusepa, Wurunsemu, Taru, Telipinu, Inara, Arinna, Hepat, Teshub only as Hurrian). Treat 'Thousand-God Court' as a calque of Hittite siunas hantezzi... i.e. 'the thousand gods' (LI-IM DINGIR-LIM, Hitt. 1000 DINGIR.MEŠ); the numeral 'thousand' is written logographically so a Hittite reading is conjectural.
